Tertullian
ter-TUL-ee-un
proper noun (church history / patristics / apologetics)
Latin name Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus; born in Carthage (North Africa, modern Tunisia) circa 155–160 AD; son of a Roman centurion; trained as a lawyer and rhetorician; converted to Christianity circa 195–197 AD; became one of the most prolific and combative theological writers of the early church; he is the “father of Latin theology” and the first major Christian writer to work principally in Latin; around 207 AD he affiliated with the Montanist movement, though he may have eventually separated from it; died circa 220–240 AD

See also: Tertullian

Biblical Definition

Tertullian of Carthage is the most important Latin-speaking theologian before Augustine, the coiner of the Latin terminology (trinitas, tres personae, una substantia) that became the standard vocabulary of Trinitarian theology, and the most vigorous apologist against Roman paganism, Gnosticism, and Marcionite Christianity in the late second and early third centuries. His apologetic posture is encapsulated in his famous rhetorical question: “What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?” — a rejection of the synthesis of Greek philosophy with Christian revelation that many later theologians pursued. His Apology (197 AD) is the most rhetorically powerful defense of Christianity against Roman legal persecution. His Against Marcion (five books) demolished the Marcionite rejection of the Old Testament and showed the unity of the two Testaments in the one God of both creation and redemption. His Against Praxeas articulated the Trinitarian doctrine that the three persons share one substance — the first precise Latin formulation. His Galatians 1:8 application was strict: any departure from the apostolic preaching, even by an angel, is to be rejected. His eventual Montanism is a caution: the most gifted theologian of his era allowed a fascination with prophetic gifts and moral rigorism to lead him outside the apostolic tradition. The Reformed tradition honors his theological contributions while reckoning soberly with his trajectory.

Webster 1828 Definition

TERTULLIAN: Latin theologian of Carthage (c. 155–220 AD); father of Latin theology; coined trinitas and the Trinitarian formula tres personae, una substantia; his apologetic writings defended Christianity against Rome and Gnosticism; his later Montanism is a warning against prophetic enthusiasm eclipsing apostolic normativity.

TERTULLIAN. n. [L. Tertullianus.] Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus; born Carthage, North Africa, c. 155–160 AD; lawyer and rhetorician by training; converted to Christianity c. 195 AD; the most prolific early Latin theological writer, producing approximately thirty works that survive.

His Trinitarian contribution: Against Praxeas (c. 213 AD) introduced trinitas (Trinity) and tres personae, una substantia (three persons, one substance) as the Latin vocabulary for the doctrine that both Sabellianism (which collapsed the persons into modes) and Adoptionism (which denied the Son's eternal divinity) distorted. This vocabulary was adopted by all subsequent Latin theology through Augustine, the Nicene Creed's Latin reception, and the Western church.

His apologetics: the Apology (197 AD) argued that Roman persecution of Christians was legally unjust and theologically perverse; Christians prayed for the emperor and held the empire together; their refusal to sacrifice to the gods was not rebellion but conscience. It is the most legally sophisticated defense of Christianity in the patristic period.

His Montanism: c. 207 AD Tertullian affiliated with the Montanist movement, which claimed continuing prophetic revelation through the “New Prophecy” of Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla. His reasons appear to have been moral rigorism (Montanism was stricter on marriage, fasting, and flight from persecution) and a genuine interest in the Spirit's ongoing work. The Reformed assessment is that Tertullian allowed the desire for a purer church and heightened spiritual experience to lead him beyond the apostolic tradition he had defended.

His famous epigrams: “The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church” (Apologeticus 50); “What has Athens to do with Jerusalem? What the Academy with the Church?” (Prescription Against Heretics 7); “I believe because it is absurd” (credo quia absurdum) — often cited but actually a paraphrase of a more nuanced statement about the resurrection.

Key Scripture

Matt 28:19 — "Go therefore and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit —"

John 14:16 — "And I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Helper — the Paraclete — to be with you forever,"

Gal 1:8 — "But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel contrary to what we have preached to you — let him be accursed!"

2 Cor 3:6 — "who also made us adequate as servants of a new covenant — not of the letter, but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The recovery needed is dual: honoring Tertullian's genuine theological contributions (Trinitarian vocabulary, apologetics) while soberly noting his Montanist departure as a warning for any era that privileges extraordinary spiritual experience over apostolic normativity.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The recovery principle here is proper attribution and balanced judgment. Contemporary charismatic and Pentecostal historiography has sometimes claimed Tertullian as an early endorsement of continuing prophecy and tongues-speech, citing his Montanist phase. The sober Reformed reading is different: Tertullian's Montanism was a deviation from the apostolic normativity he had himself defended, not an endorsement of the New Prophecy as a permanent fixture. The same man who wrote that nothing may be added to the apostolic preaching (the Prescription's argument) later affiliated with a movement that claimed ongoing revelation supplementing that preaching. The contradiction is the warning.

A subtler corruption comes from the over-citation of Tertullian's “What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?” as a proof-text for anti-intellectualism or for the rejection of any engagement with philosophy and culture. Tertullian's actual argument is narrower: the specific forms of Hellenistic speculative philosophy that had produced Gnostic Christianity were incompatible with the apostolic rule of faith. He did not argue that reason, logic, or cultural engagement were illegitimate; he argued that autonomous Greek philosophy was not the norming standard for Christian doctrine. The Reformed apologetic tradition (Bavinck, Van Til, Frame) has appropriated this point without endorsing wholesale cultural withdrawal.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin Tertullianus; trained lawyer and rhetorician; North African Christian apologist and theologian (c. 155–220 AD); coiner of trinitas and the Trinitarian formula; his Montanist phase a cautionary instance of rigorism and prophetic enthusiasm departing from apostolic normativity.

expand to see more

Legal rhetorical formation — Tertullian's training as a Roman lawyer gave his theological writing its characteristic precision, adversarial energy, and argument-from-precedent structure; the Apology reads like a legal brief; Against Marcion reads like a prosecution; this legal cast shaped Latin theology's distinctive doctrinal precision

Trinitas (Trinity) — Tertullian's coinage in Against Praxeas: the first Latin use of the term for the threeness of God; his formula tres personae, una substantia (three persons, one substance) became the permanent Western Trinitarian vocabulary, carried through Augustine, the Nicene Creed's Latin formulation, and the medieval scholastics

Praescriptio haereticorum (Prescription Against Heretics) — Tertullian's forensic argument that heresy has no standing to appeal to the Scriptures, because the Scriptures belong to the churches that have preserved the apostolic tradition; the heretic who builds on Scripture is squatting on another's property; a characteristically legal argument with genuinely patristic ecclesiological implications

North African Christianity — Tertullian is the founding figure of a distinctive North African theological tradition that continued through Cyprian and Augustine; this tradition was characterized by moral rigorism, high ecclesiology, and close attention to the church's visible boundary; its influence on Augustine's doctrine of the church and the sacraments was enormous

Montanism as cautionary trajectory — the movement (second century, Phrygia) claimed the Spirit was speaking through Montanus and his prophetesses with binding revelations supplementing the apostolic deposit; Tertullian's affiliation represents the failure mode of a church that has reduced the apostolic tradition to external rules rather than making it a living framework for discernment: he was seeking a purer, more Spirit-filled community and found it in a place that departed from the apostolic deposit he had defended

Usage

"Tertullian's Trinitarian contribution is practically indispensable: every time a Reformed congregation confesses the Trinity in the language of three persons and one substance, they are using vocabulary Tertullian coined. Preaching through Trinitarian doctrine should note this lineage: the precise language Christians use for the most fundamental claim about God was forged in the crucible of second-century controversy by a North African lawyer defending the faith against those who would collapse the persons or deny the Son's co-eternity."

"His Montanist trajectory is the Reformed tradition's cautionary template for evaluating charismatic movements that claim special prophetic revelation supplementing the apostolic deposit. The argument for the New Prophecy in Tertullian's day is structurally identical to contemporary arguments for the “prophetic movement”: the Spirit is speaking fresh words; a stricter holiness is required; ordinary church life has become too settled and accommodated. The Galatians 1:8 principle applies: even if an angel from heaven, even if Tertullian himself in his Montanist phase — if it contradicts the apostolic preaching, let it be accursed."

"The “Athens and Jerusalem” question is a perennial apologetic resource but must be handled carefully. Tertullian's point is not that Christians should be ignorant of philosophy or disengaged from culture; it is that the church's rule of faith — the apostolic deposit — is the norm, not the Academy's assumptions. Engaging philosophy, science, literature, and culture is legitimate and necessary; allowing philosophical assumptions to revise the apostolic content is heresy. The Reformed tradition has consistently held this distinction."
